name: Discourse Connective Analysis
description: Analyzes discourse connective usage patterns and distribution — AI overuses certain connectives while underusing others.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated text by analyzing the selection and distribution of discourse connectives — words and phrases that signal logical relationships between text segments. AI text shows characteristic connective overuse/underuse patterns that differ from human writing:

1. **Connective Inventory and Frequency Profiling**: The method identifies all discourse connectives (conjunctions, adverbials, prepositional phrases) and classifies them by discourse relation type using the Penn Discourse TreeBank (PDTB) taxonomy: (a) temporal — "then", "subsequently", "meanwhile", "previously", (b) causal — "because", "therefore", "consequently", "as a result", (c) contrastive — "however", "nevertheless", "on the other hand", "despite this", (d) additive — "moreover", "furthermore", "additionally", "in addition", (e) conditional — "if", "unless", "provided that", (f) elaborative — "specifically", "in particular", "for example". The method computes frequency per 1000 words for each category. AI text characteristically overuses additive connectives ("moreover", "furthermore" — 2–3× human rate) and contrastive connectives ("however" — 1.5–2× human rate), while underusing temporal and conditional connectives. The connective-to-sentence ratio: human text 0.3–0.5; AI text 0.5–0.8 (AI over-marks discourse relations that should be implicit).

2. **Connective Repetition and Vocabulary Breadth**: The method measures connective diversity: (a) unique connective types — human text uses 20–35 distinct connective types per 2000 words; AI text uses 10–18, recycling a small set. (b) Connective type-token ratio — similar to lexical TTR but for connectives only. Human: 0.5–0.7; AI: 0.3–0.5. (c) Top-3 concentration — what proportion of all connective tokens come from the three most-used connectives. Human: 25–40%; AI: 45–65% (heavily concentrated on "however", "moreover", and "therefore"/"furthermore"). (d) Rare connective usage — connectives like "notwithstanding", "inasmuch as", "by the same token" that appear in sophisticated human writing but almost never in AI text. Human: 1–3 rare connectives per 2000 words; AI: < 0.5.

3. **Connective Position and Scope Analysis**: Where a connective appears in its clause affects its discourse function. The method tracks: (a) clause position — initial ("However, the results..."), medial ("The results, however, showed..."), final ("...the results showed, however"). Human text distributes: 65% initial, 25% medial, 10% final. AI text: > 85% initial, < 12% medial, < 3% final. AI almost always places connectives at clause start. (b) Scope — some connectives can have different scopes (intra-sentential vs. inter-sentential). "But" can link clauses within a sentence or link sentences. The method checks whether scope is appropriate: AI sometimes uses inter-sentential connectives ("Furthermore") for intra-sentential relations, creating an overly formal tone. (c) Paired connectives — "on the one hand...on the other hand", "not only...but also" — human text uses 1–3 paired connectives per 1000 words; AI uses < 0.5.

4. **Connective-Relation Congruence**: The method checks whether connectives match the actual discourse relation between the segments they connect: (a) signal-relation alignment — using an NLI model to independently classify the discourse relation, then checking if the connective matches. Human text shows > 85% congruence; AI text shows 70–80% (AI sometimes uses contrastive connectives where no contrast exists, or causal connectives for mere temporal sequences). (b) Unnecessary connectives — discourse relations that are obvious without explicit marking ("She was tired. Therefore, she went to bed" — the causal relation is self-evident). Human text leaves obvious relations unmarked; AI text tends to over-mark. (c) Missing connectives — complex discourse relations that need explicit marking but are left unmarked. Human text makes sophisticated judgments about when to mark; AI text either over-marks or under-marks, rarely finding the right balance.
parameters:
Connective taxonomy: PDTB (6 relation types)
Human connective rate: 0.3–0.5 per sentence
AI connective rate: 0.5–0.8 per sentence
Human unique connectives: 20–35 per 2000 words
AI unique connectives: 10–18 per 2000 words
Top-3 concentration human: 25–40%
Top-3 concentration AI: 45–65%
Initial position human: ~65%
Initial position AI: > 85%
Signal-relation congruence human: > 85%
Minimum text length: 400 words
accuracy: 79–88% accuracy detecting AI-generated text via discourse connective analysis. Connective vocabulary breadth achieves AUC of 0.85. Position analysis adds 2–3% improvement. Connective-relation congruence provides F1-score of 0.83. Performance best for expository and argumentative text.
source: Prasad, R. et al. (2008). The Penn Discourse TreeBank 2.0. LREC 2008.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated essays and articles through connective overuse patterns. Evaluating discourse coherence quality. Identifying AI-written reports through formulaic connective usage. Academic integrity checking for student essays.
strengths:
• Discourse connectives are a well-studied, finite set of markers
• AI overuse of "however/moreover/furthermore" is a strong signal
• Position analysis captures syntactic flexibility that AI lacks
• Congruence checking evaluates genuine logical reasoning
• Easily interpretable results for human reviewers
limitations:
• Some genres (academic writing) naturally use many discourse connectives
• Non-native English writers may show similar connective patterns to AI
• Short texts may not contain enough connectives for reliable analysis
• Advanced AI models can be prompted to vary connective usage
• Register differences affect expected connective distributions
